cards.subject: ent
cards.stem: Ear station: a patient with a sebaceous cyst / dermoid cyst.
answer: (a) 1. Epidermoid Cyst: Similar to sebaceous cysts but lack sebaceous glands.
2. Preauricular Sinus Abscess: Congenital pit near the ear that can become infected.
3. Auricular Hematoma: Collection of blood between the ear cartilage and skin.
4. Lipoma: A benign fatty tumor that can occur in the ear or surrounding areas.
5. Chronic Otitis Externa with Abscess: Can present as a swelling near the ear.
1. Clinical Examination: Inspection and palpation to assess consistency, mobility, and signs of infection.
2. Ultrasound of the Lesion: helps differentiate between cystic and solid masses.
3. Fine Needle Aspiration Cytology (FNAC): can confirm sebaceous or dermoid cyst.
4. CT Scan or MRI (if needed) of the head: To rule out deep-seated or congenital anomalies, especially in dermoid cysts.
5. Histopathology (after excision): Definitive diagnosis confirming the nature of the cyst.
1. Conservative Management: Small, asymptomatic cysts may be observed.
2. Incision and Drainage: If infected, drainage is done followed by antibiotics.
(i) For sebaceous cysts: Ensures removal of the cyst wall to prevent recurrence.
(ii) For dermoid cysts: Requires complete excision due to potential deeper involvement.
4. Antibiotics and Anti-inflammatory Medication: If there is secondary infection.
5. Postoperative Care: Wound care, follow-up to check for recurrence.
refs: 1. Mohan Bansal – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery. Page 187-190: (Sebaceous and dermoid cysts of the ear).
2. Dhingra & Dhingra – Diseases of Ear, Nose, and Throat (8th ed.) Page 210-215:
(Benign lesions of the ear, including cysts).
3. Scott-Brown’s Otorhinolaryngology and Head & Neck Surgery (8th ed.) Volume 1, Page 500-505: (Differential diagnosis and management of ear cysts).

cards.subject: ent
cards.stem: Nose station: a patient with turbinate hypertrophy.
answer: (a) 1. Allergic Rhinitis: Chronic inflammation due to allergens causing turbinate swelling.
2. Chronic Rhinosinusitis: Persistent inflammation and congestion leading to turbinate enlargement.
3. Nasal Polyps: Soft, painless growths that can mimic turbinate hypertrophy.
4. Deviated Nasal Septum (DNS) with Compensatory Hypertrophy: One turbinate enlarges due to septal deviation.
5. Hormonal Rhinitis (Pregnancy or Hypothyroidism-related): Caused by hormonal fluctuations leading to nasal congestion.
1. Anterior Rhinoscopy: Direct visualization of the enlarged turbinates
2. Nasal Endoscopy: Provides a detailed view of the nasal cavity and helps rule out other pathologies.
3. CT Scan of the Paranasal Sinuses: To assess the extent of hypertrophy and exclude sinus pathology.
4. Allergy Testing (Skin Prick or Serum IgE Levels): To check for allergic rhinitis.
5. Rhinomanometry: Measures nasal airflow and resistance to assess obstruction severity.
(i) Intranasal Corticosteroids (Fluticasone, Mometasone): Reduce inflammation and turbinate size.
(ii) Antihistamines (Loratadine, Cetirizine): Useful in allergic rhinitis.
(iii) Nasal Decongestants (Oxymetazoline, Xylometazoline): Short-term relief but risk of rebound congestion (rhinitis medicamentosa).
(iv) Saline Nasal Irrigation: Clears allergens and mucus, improving symptoms.
(a) Turbinate Reduction Surgery: These techniques include;
(i) Submucosal Diathermy (SMD): Shrinks the turbinate by heat application.
(ii) Radiofrequency Ablation (RFA): Minimally invasive method for reducing turbinate size.
(iii) Partial Turbinectomy: Surgical removal of part of the hypertrophied turbinate.
(iv) Coblation Turbinoplasty: Uses plasma technology to reduce turbinate tissue with minimal damage.
refs: 1. Mohan Bansal – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery Page 275-280: (Turbinate hypertrophy, causes, and treatment).
2. Dhingra & Dhingra – Diseases of Ear, Nose, and Throat (8th ed.) Page 225-230: (Turbinate disorders and their management).
3. Scott-Brown’s Otorhinolaryngology and Head & Neck Surgery (8th ed.) Volume 2, Page 1100-1105: (Pathophysiology and surgical treatment of turbinate hypertrophy).

cards.subject: ent
cards.stem: Throat station: a patient with pharyngitis / tonsillitis.
answer: (a) 1. Infectious Mononucleosis (Epstein-Barr Virus - EBV): Presents with sore throat, fever, lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly.
2. Diphtheria: Grayish-white pseudomembrane over the tonsils, systemic toxicity.
3. Peritonsillar Abscess (Quinsy): Unilateral tonsillar swelling, trismus, and uvular deviation.
4. Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD): Chronic sore throat due to acid reflux, worse in the morning.
5. Hand-Foot-Mouth Disease (Coxsackievirus A16): Oral ulcers, fever, and vesicular rash on hands and feet.
1. Throat Swab Culture & Sensitivity: To identify bacterial pathogens (e.g., Group A Streptococcus).
2. Complete Blood Count (CBC): Elevated WBCs indicate bacterial infection, lymphocytosis suggests viral etiology.
3. Monospot Test (Heterophile Antibody Test): Confirms infectious mononucleosis.
4. Anti-Streptolysin O (ASO) Titer: Helps diagnose post-streptococcal complications like rheumatic fever.
5. Lateral Neck X-ray (if needed): To rule out epiglottitis in severe airway obstruction.
• Dexamethasone for airway edema in severe cases.
• Acyclovir (if severe Herpes Simplex Virus infection).
2. Surgical Management (If Recurrent or Complicated Cases):
• Recurrent tonsillitis (>7 episodes in 1 year, >5/year for 2 years, >3/year for 3 years).
• Peritonsillar abscess (recurrent or unresponsive to treatment).
(ii) Abscess Drainage: Needle aspiration or incision & drainage for peritonsillar abscess.
refs: 1. Mohan Bansal – Diseases of Ear, Nose and Throat & Head and Neck Surgery Page 310-320: (Tonsillitis, differential diagnosis, and management).
2. Dhingra & Dhingra – Diseases of Ear, Nose, and Throat (8th ed.) Page 255-265: (Pharyngitis, tonsillitis, and their complications).
3. Scott-Brown’s Otorhinolaryngology and Head & Neck Surgery (8th ed.) Volume 2, Page 1200-1215: (Acute and chronic tonsillitis, surgical indications, and techniques).

prompts: What is the name of this procedure?
answer: (Take note of the strings hanging from the other end).
a. Discomfort and Pain: Nasal packing can cause significant discomfort, requiring analgesia.
b. Nasal Obstruction and Mouth Breathing: Leads to dryness of the mouth and throat irritation.
c. Septal Necrosis and Perforation: Excessive pressure from packing can cause ischemia, leading to necrosis and perforation of the nasal septum.
d. Mucosal Injury and Adhesions: Removal of packing may cause mucosal trauma, increasing the risk of synechiae (nasal adhesions).
a. Sinusitis: Nasal packing obstructs normal sinus drainage, leading to bacterial growth and secondary sinus infections.
b. Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS): A rare but life-threatening complication caused by Staphylococcus aureus toxin production.(Symptoms: High fever, hypotension, rash, and multi-organ failure.)
a. Hypoxia and Sleep Apnea: Nasal obstruction can worsen pre-existing sleep apnea or cause transient hypoxia, especially in elderly or comorbid patients.
b. Reflex Bradycardia (Vasovagal Response): Pressure on the nasal mucosa can stimulate the trigeminal nerve, leading to bradycardia, hypotension, and syncope.
c. Aspiration and Airway Compromise: Posterior displacement of packing can cause airway obstruction, particularly in unconscious or sedated patients.
